name: Statue of Liberty
info: The Statue of Liberty is a colossal copper-clad statue of a robed woman on Liberty Island in New York Harbor, designed by Bartholdi with a framework by Gustave Eiffel and given by the people of France to the United States, dedicated in 1886.

facts.made: Designed by the French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, with Eugène Viollet-le-Duc as first chief engineer and Gustave Eiffel as builder of the framework; paid for by French donors, with the pedestal by Richard Morris Hunt paid for by Americans
facts.form: A neoclassical figure of Libertas in repoussé copper sheets about 2.4 mm thick on an iron framework, Bartholdi having decided on a height of just over 151 feet (46 m), set on a granite-faced concrete pedestal 89 feet (27 m) high
facts.where: On Liberty Island, formerly Bedloe's Island, in Upper New York Bay, part of New York City and of the Statue of Liberty National Monument
facts.known: the torch and the tabula ansata inscribed JULY IV MDCCLXXVI; the broken chain at her feet; Emma Lazarus's sonnet The New Colossus; its role as a symbol of welcome to immigrants; Eiffel's curtain wall construction; the 1986 restoration; the green patina of verdigris

t: The statue was proposed by the French abolitionist Édouard de Laboulaye as a gift marking American independence and the end of slavery; the French people paid for it and Americans paid for the pedestal.
Eiffel replaced a planned masonry pier with an iron truss tower, so that the copper skin hangs from a framework that lets it move slightly in the wind, an early example of curtain wall construction.
Built as a symbol of liberty and republican ideals, it came to be seen by arriving immigrants as a sign of welcome, a reading that Emma Lazarus's sonnet of 1883 had anticipated.
dyk: Bartholdi considered having Liberty hold a broken chain and decided it would be too divisive after the Civil War, so the statue strides over a chain half-hidden by her robes and difficult to see from the ground.
ev: Laboulaye announced the project and the Franco-American Union to raise money in France
The torch-bearing arm was shown at the Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia and then in Madison Square Park
The French steamer Isère brought the disassembled statue to New York in crates
The statue was dedicated in a ceremony presided over by President Grover Cleveland
The Black Tom explosion damaged the torch-bearing arm, and the climb to the torch was closed for good
President Calvin Coolidge declared the statue a national monument
The statue was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site
After a restoration that replaced the whole iron armature and the torch, the statue was rededicated

sections.origins:
The idea of a monument given by the French people to the United States is traced to Édouard René de Laboulaye, president of the French Anti-Slavery Society and an ardent supporter of the Union in the American Civil War. A mid-1865 conversation with the sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi is the usual starting point, but the National Park Service, in a report of 2000, deemed that story a legend traced to an 1885 fundraising pamphlet and judged that the statue was most likely conceived in 1870. Laboulaye proposed a monument to mark the centennial of American independence, the perseverance of American democracy and the liberation of the nation's slaves.

Bartholdi took no immediate action under the regime of Napoleon III. In the late 1860s he had proposed to Isma'il Pasha, Khedive of Egypt, a huge lighthouse in the form of a robed peasant woman holding a torch at the entrance to the Suez Canal; the khedive and Ferdinand de Lesseps declined it because of the cost. After the Franco-Prussian War, in which Bartholdi served as a major of militia and his home province of Alsace was lost, he crossed the Atlantic in June 1871 with letters of introduction from Laboulaye. He chose Bedloe's Island as the site, struck by the fact that every vessel arriving in New York had to sail past it.
sections.content:
The statue, titled Liberty Enlightening the World, is a colossal neoclassical figure of a classically draped woman inspired by Libertas, the Roman goddess of freedom. She holds a torch above her head in her right hand. In her left she carries a tabula ansata, a tablet used to evoke the concept of law, inscribed JULY IV MDCCLXXVI, the date of the Declaration of Independence. Her raised right foot is set back in a contrapposto pose, and she steps on a broken chain and shackle commemorating the abolition of slavery after the Civil War. Bartholdi gave her a radiate halo in place of the liberty cap, the pileus given to freed slaves in Rome, which would have recalled the figure of Marianne. Many have believed that the rays evoke the sun, the seven seas and the seven continents, but research has not confirmed this.

Bartholdi and Laboulaye avoided the image of revolutionary liberty in Delacroix's Liberty Leading the People, in which a half-clothed Liberty leads an armed mob. Laboulaye had no sympathy for revolution, so the figure is fully dressed, and the torch, representing progress, gives it a peaceful appearance. Bartholdi wrote that the surfaces should be broad and simple. Popular accounts say the face was modelled on his mother, but the curator of the Bartholdi Museum has said that this and similar speculations have no basis in fact.
sections.making:
In September 1875 Laboulaye announced the project and the Franco-American Union, its fundraising arm. The French people were to finance the statue, contrary to the misconception that the French national government paid for it, and Americans were to pay for the pedestal. Gifts came from schoolchildren, ordinary citizens and 181 French municipalities, and the French government authorised a lottery. Bartholdi built the right arm and the head first, with Eugène Viollet-le-Duc as chief engineer. Viollet-le-Duc chose copper sheets about 2.4 mm thick, shaped by repoussé, in which the sheets were heated and struck with wooden hammers, at the workshop of Gaget, Gauthier and Co.

Viollet-le-Duc died in 1879 without saying how he meant to join the copper skin to his proposed masonry pier. Gustave Eiffel and his engineer Maurice Koechlin replaced it with an iron truss tower and a secondary skeleton joined to the skin by flat iron bars and riveted saddles, so that the statue could move slightly in the wind. Eiffel insulated the skin with asbestos impregnated with shellac to prevent galvanic corrosion. The statue was presented to the American ambassador in Paris on 4 July 1884. In the United States, Richard Morris Hunt designed the pedestal, which was cut from 114 to 89 feet for lack of money, and the engineer Joachim Goschen Giæver prepared the structural framework from Eiffel's drawings.
sections.reception:
The announcement of 1875 drew a generally favourable reaction in France, though many French people resented the United States for not coming to their aid in the war with Prussia, and monarchists opposed the statue because the liberal Laboulaye had proposed it. In the United States fundraising for the pedestal lagged. Critics disliked the idea that Americans should pay the bill, and after the Civil War most preferred realistic works showing national heroes to allegory. The New York Times stated that no true patriot could countenance such expenditures for bronze females. Grover Cleveland, as governor of New York, vetoed a bill for 50,000 dollars in 1884, and groups from Boston and Philadelphia offered to pay for the statue in return for moving it.

Joseph Pulitzer's newspaper, the New York World, then ran a drive that by 11 August 1885 had raised 102,000 dollars from 120,000 donors, 80 percent of it in sums under a dollar. At the dedication on 28 October 1886, only dignitaries were allowed on the island and the only women admitted were Bartholdi's wife and Lesseps's granddaughter; suffragists chartered a boat and spoke in favour of women's right to vote. The Cleveland Gazette, an African American newspaper, suggested that the torch not be lit until the United States became a free nation in reality, citing the Ku Klux Klan and murder of Black citizens. Many immigrants arriving in the late 19th and early 20th centuries saw the statue as a sign of welcome.
sections.survival:
The torch gave only a faint gleam at the dedication, and the Lighthouse Board, which took over in 1887, could not make the statue a useful light. President Theodore Roosevelt moved it to the War Department in 1901. By 1906 a green patina of verdigris had covered the statue; believing it to be corrosion, Congress authorised money for repairs and for painting the statue inside and out, but the Army Corps of Engineers concluded that the patina protected the copper, and the statue was painted only on the inside. In 1916 German saboteurs set off an explosion on the Black Tom peninsula that caused minor damage, mostly to the torch-bearing arm; the narrow ascent to the torch has been closed since. Gutzon Borglum then redesigned the torch with stained glass, and floodlights were installed. The statue passed to the National Park Service in 1933, and the Works Progress Administration carried out repairs in the late 1930s.

Studies for the centennial found that the right arm was improperly attached and swayed in strong winds, that the head had been installed 2 feet off centre and that the armature was badly corroded. The restoration of 1984 to 1986 replaced Eiffel's entire puddled iron armature with stainless steel bars of Ferralium, and replaced the torch, now covered in 24-karat gold leaf, with a replica of Bartholdi's original.
sections.legacy:
The statue became an icon of freedom and of the United States. Many immigrants who arrived by sea saw it as a sign of welcome rather than of enlightenment as Bartholdi had intended, and Ellis Island's immigration station strengthened the association. Emma Lazarus's sonnet The New Colossus, written for a fundraising auction in 1883, called the statue the Mother of Exiles and contrasted it with the Colossus of Rhodes; it was engraved on a plaque at the base in 1903. In the First World War, images of the statue appeared on recruitment posters and Liberty bond drives. UNESCO's statement of significance describes it as a potent symbol inspiring contemplation, debate and protest.

Hundreds of replicas stand around the world, among them a smaller version on the Île aux Cygnes in Paris. The Goddess of Democracy raised during the Tiananmen Square protests of 1989 was inspired by French democratic traditions, though its sculptors took care to avoid imitating the statue. Demonstrators have also used it as a stage for causes ranging from women's rights in 1970 to opposition to the Vietnam War in 1971. The historian Maria Cristina Garcia says that the chains being barely visible is why Americans have forgotten this history.

summary: The Statue of Liberty is a copper statue designed by Bartholdi, built over an iron framework by Gustave Eiffel, and given by the French people to the United States. Dedicated in 1886, it was first meant to mark independence and the end of slavery, and came to be read as a welcome to immigrants.
